title: Having court fees waived
intro: This guide explains what the Ontario government says about fee waivers in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court: who can ask, who may qualify, how to apply, what is not covered and when a waiver applies.

sections.heading: What a fee waiver is
paragraphs: “You might need to pay fees if you go to court in Ontario. If you cannot afford to pay the fees, you can ask the court to waive them.” The court “will consider your financial situation and decide whether you meet the requirements to qualify.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

If the person meets the requirements “and the court agrees to waive the fees”, they get “a certificate called a fee waiver.” The page says to “Show this certificate to court staff if they ask you to pay a fee.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

“There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.” “You need to apply for a separate fee waiver for each case or proceeding you are involved in. A fee waiver will not apply to any fees you have already paid.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

“Each request is reviewed based on the form and documents you submit. The decision of staff or a judge is final. If your financial situation changes, you can request a fee waiver again.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: Who can ask, and who may qualify
paragraphs: A person can ask for a fee waiver if they “are or will be involved in a family, civil or small claims court matter”, “are not acting on behalf of a business or organization”, and their fees “are not being paid by a lawyer under a contingency fee agreement”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

The court may approve the request if the main source of household income is from Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program, the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the War Veterans Allowance, or Canada Pension Plan benefits. It may also approve it if “your lawyer is being paid by a Legal Aid Certificate”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

The financial requirements refer to “gross annual household income”, meaning what everyone in the household earns in a year before taxes or deductions. The page says it must be below $33,100 for one person, $49,600 for two people, $57,300 for three people, $68,700 for four people, and $80,200 for five or more people. It also lists household liquid assets of less than $2,800 and household net worth of less than $11,100. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

Listed with the income limits, as part of the same financial eligibility requirements, are “your household liquid assets are less than $2,800” and “your household net worth is less than $11,100”. Net worth is “the value of all assets owned by the members of your household, minus their debts and other financial liabilities”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

A person who does not meet the requirements but does not believe they can afford the fees “can make a request directly to the court to have your financial situation evaluated by a judge.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: What a fee waiver does not cover
paragraphs: Fees that cannot be waived include “fees you pay to someone who is not part of the court (this includes lawyers, authorized court transcriptionists, official examiners, witnesses and mediators)”, “fees relating to criminal matters”, “the federal Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings fee”, and “fees for serving documents on another party”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

Also excluded are disbursements paid to the sheriff or small claims court bailiff to enforce an order (with one exception for orders under subsection 31(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006), and fees prescribed for bankruptcy proceedings. “A fee waiver does not apply to any costs a court has ordered you to pay to another party.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: How to apply: the forms and documents
paragraphs: A person who thinks they meet the financial requirements uses the Fee Waiver Request to Registrar, Clerk or Sheriff (form FW-A-3). A person who does not think they meet them uses the Fee Waiver Request to Court (form FW-A 4). Forms FW-A 6 and FW-A 7 are the versions for a litigation guardian or special party representative. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
The applicant must “provide proof of your gross annual household income. This includes proof of income for your spouse, if you have one.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

For form FW-A-3 or FW-A 6, any one of three documents may be given for the applicant and for their spouse: the tax return or notice of assessment for the most recent tax year; the most recent employer statement of earnings or three most recent pay stubs; or the most recent statement of income from employment insurance, social assistance, a pension, workers compensation or disability payments. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

“If you cannot provide any of these documents, explain why and continue to fill out the rest of the form”. No proof of income is needed “if your lawyer is being paid by a Legal Aid Certificate.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

With form FW-A 4 or FW-A 7, the applicant fills out Exhibit B listing household members’ income, expenses and assets, with a recent financial document for each item. With Exhibit C, they provide the first document filed in the case showing their position, or “a copy of the order you wish to enforce or continue enforcing”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

The page describes a Guided Pathway for requesting a court fee waiver as “a free online tool developed by Community Legal Education Ontario ( CLEO ) and the Ministry of the Attorney General.” It “asks you questions and inserts your answers into the required court form.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: Swearing, submitting and timing
paragraphs: The applicant “must swear or affirm that the information you provided is accurate and true to the best of your knowledge.” This can be done “for free at the court or enforcement office”, or by a lawyer, paralegal, notary public or commissioner for taking affidavits, who may charge a fee. “It is a criminal offence to knowingly swear or affirm a false affidavit.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

The request can be submitted online, by mail or in person. “You can submit the form on its own or along with any court document that you wish to file.” A lawyer or representative can also submit it. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

By mail, the form goes to the court or enforcement office where the fee would be paid, and “You will get a response in the mail.” In person, “You will find out immediately if you qualify for the fee waiver.” More generally, the page says: “Court staff will review your request first. If they determine that you do not meet the requirements, your request will be presented to a judge for review.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

Online, “If you have a fee waiver or want to apply for a fee waiver, you must use the online portals listed above when submitting your documents.” Toronto-region filings use the Ontario Courts Public Portal; other regions use the Justice Services Online portal. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: After a fee waiver is granted
paragraphs: A fee waiver “can be revoked (cancelled or invalidated) by a judge if they think that your actions in your case or proceeding are frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of the court’s process.” A judge can also require the person to get permission before asking for another fee waiver. “You will have a chance to submit a statement or argument to a judge before they revoke your fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

With a fee waiver, a person “can request the help of a court interpreter for free for any language other than English or French”, for themselves or a witness, using form FW-A 5. The form is to be submitted “as soon as you find out the date and time of the court appearance when the interpreter will be required.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

sections.heading: Small Claims Court
paragraphs: “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” In the part of the page on filing in the Toronto region through the Ontario Courts Public Portal, it says “you must indicate if you have a fee waiver or want to apply for a fee waiver”, and to select “Request fee waiver” when applying for a certificate at the same time. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)

In the part of the page on filing outside the Toronto region through the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal, it describes two choices for a document that would normally have a fee: “Fee waiver request” when applying for a certificate at the same time, or “Document is being submitted by a person with a fee waiver certificate” when a certificate is already held. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)

In its section on a summonsed witness who needs an interpreter, the Ministry’s trial guide says the court provides English-French and visual language interpretation, that the party summonsing the witness arranges interpretation for other languages, and that “The court will provide an interpreter for other languages to parties who have qualified for a fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)

sections.heading: Superior Court of Justice (civil)
paragraphs: “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)

For filing outside the Toronto region, the page says: “If you have a fee waiver or want to apply for one, you must use the Civil Submissions Online portal below to submit your documents.” It adds that “The Civil Claims Online portal will not apply the relevant fee exemptions. You will not receive a fee refund if you file a document using Civil Claims Online.” (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)

In the Civil Submissions Online portal (outside the Toronto region), to apply together with a document, the filer selects “Fee waiver request” for any document that usually requires a fee. A filer who already has a certificate chooses “Document is being submitted by a person with a fee waiver certificate”. (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)

sections.heading: Family court
paragraphs: The general fee waiver rules above apply to a person who is “involved in a family, civil or small claims court matter”. The Guided Pathway for requesting a court fee waiver is listed under Guided Pathways to Family Court Forms. The page notes that the federal Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings fee cannot be waived. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

The site does not yet have a source on how fee waivers are handled when filing family court documents online. The general page says that anyone who has or wants a fee waiver “must use the online portals listed above when submitting your documents”, choosing the fee waiver option for any document requiring a fee, and links to a separate page on filing family court documents online. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
